1:
The undefined interval is noticed first. Robertson allows that a whole year may lie between the events of the previous chapter and these in Galilee, and sees no reason to think the chapters once stood in the other order; Wesley says ten or eleven months of history must be supplied from the other evangelists. Ellicott declines both the arbitrary supposition that a portion of the Gospel has been lost and the attempt to connect the chapters in immediate sequence, since for John the discourse is what the whole is recorded for; the exact order of events he leaves undetermined. Calvin explains why the miracle appears here at all, against John's custom of supplying what the others omit: he repeats it expressly in order to pass from it to the sermon delivered next day at Capernaum.

Chrysostom takes the retirement for a lesson in method: missiles rebound with great force from a hard body where a softer material stops them, so violent men are only excited to greater rage by violence and are softened by gentleness, and Christ quieted the irritation of the Jews by withdrawing from Jerusalem.

On the provisions the eye-witness detail is what the commentators prize. Ellicott observes that John alone knows the loaves were barley, the ordinary black bread of the Galilean peasant, and that they belonged not to the disciples but to a lad who had followed the crowd hoping to find a purchaser. Clarke supplies the economics, barley bearing scarcely a third of the value of wheat, and cites the handfuls of barley for which false prophetesses polluted the name of God as the measure of so mean a fare. Robertson notes the diminutive for the boy occurs only here in the New Testament. Gill leaves open whether the lad belonged to Christ and the disciples, which would show how meanly they lived, or came to sell. Lightfoot sets it beside Elisha's feeding, where the rabbis enlarge the number fed to two thousand two hundred, a loaf set before every hundred men.

The question put to Philip is peculiar to this Gospel, and two of them say why. Ellicott contrasts the standpoints: the earlier narratives show the scene from the outer circle, where the request comes from the disciples, John from within. Calvin removes the inconsistency by supposing that Philip spoke according to the opinion entertained by all, so what is here addressed to one the others attribute to the company. Wesley guesses that Philip had the care of providing victuals for the apostles.

The thanksgiving draws a comment out of Calvin: Christ instructs us by his example that whenever we take food we ought to begin with prayer, since what God appoints for our use is evidence of his fatherly love and calls on us to praise him. Robertson identifies it as the ordinary grace before meals, where the Synoptics use the word blessed.

The crowd's conclusion and its consequence close the passage. Barnes and Clarke identify the prophet as the Messiah promised in Deuteronomy, Clarke remarking how near these people were at that moment to the kingdom of heaven; Robertson calls the verb inchoative, that they began to say it, and detects a movement to start a revolution against Rome. Calvin allows some ground for giving Christ the title of king and puts the error elsewhere, in their taking on themselves the liberty of appointing one, which Scripture ascribes to God alone, and in the earthly kingdom they contrived. Henry calls it irregular zeal in Christ's followers; Barnes traces it to their supposing the Messiah a temporal prince; Bede puts the motive plainly, that men like a merciful king to rule over them and a powerful one to protect them. Ellicott observes that Matthew and Mark record only that he withdrew to pray, not knowing the reason John gives; Gill, that he perceived their purpose as the God who knows the heart.
16:
The hour is fixed before anything else. Robertson distinguishes this late evening, the real one, from the mid-afternoon evening of the earlier narrative, and notes that the disciples were in no hurry to start back; Gill makes the same division, the first of the evenings having fallen before they sat down to eat. Calvin supplies the reason for the separation: Christ meant to conceal himself until the crowd dispersed, since a popular tumult is not easily allayed and a stain once fixed on him would not easily have been wiped off, and he spent the interval in prayer, as the other evangelists record. Chrysostom draws the pastoral point from the same fact, that Christ provides for the good of his disciples not only when present in the body but also when far away.

Where they were going is less clear than it looks. Clarke observes that Mark has them ordered to Bethsaida while in the event they landed in the country of Gennesaret, and supposes the two towns lay only a few miles apart on the same shore. Ellicott notes that the better text has not a ship but the ship, the one in which they had first crossed, and that the verb means they were going over, the voyage still continuing; he adds that Matthew speaks generally of the other side and Mark of a Bethsaida distinct from Bethsaida Julias on the east. Robertson reads the tenses as a piece of dramatic writing, two past perfects set against an imperfect, so that while they were going, darkness had already come and Jesus had not yet come to them. Calvin remarks how much John passes over that the others tell, among it the hours of struggling against a contrary wind and the fourth watch of the night.

The distance rowed is measured out. Robertson makes it a little over halfway across a lake of some six miles, and marks the shift into a graphic present when they behold him; Ellicott and Clarke both reach the same point by Josephus, who gives the lake as forty furlongs wide, Clarke adding that the vessel was small and that no sail could be carried in such a wind. Calvin explains the terror from the other narratives, that they took him for an apparition, and says it is impossible not to be seized with dread at such a sight, since we conclude it is either an imposture of Satan or some evil omen; he finds in the episode a mirror of what knowledge of Christ we can obtain without his word.

The word that quiets them is weighed for its limits. Robertson notes what John leaves out, both the apparition and Peter walking on the water. Calvin insists that it is in Christ's presence alone that we have grounds of confidence enough to be calm, but that this belongs exclusively to his disciples, since the same words afterwards struck down the wicked in the garden, he being sent as a judge to unbelievers and as a deliverer to his own.

The landing divides them. Ellicott holds that the Greek says no more than that they were willing to receive him, though Matthew and Mark state that they did, and Robertson calls the verb inchoative, that they began to be willing. Gill has them receive him the more gladly for being in distress. On what followed Clarke thinks the evangelist speaks of the sudden arrival as extraordinary and miraculous; Barnes denies there is any evidence of a miracle at all, since we do not know how far from land they were and the word rendered immediately means only that no long interval passed, as the parable of the sower uses the same word of seed springing up.
22:
The crowd is left to work out for itself what happened. Chrysostom makes that the point: Christ did not show himself walking on the sea, but gave them the means of inferring it. Calvin sets the inference out as a chain: there had been only one boat, they saw it leave without him, other boats came next day from elsewhere, and they found him at Capernaum, so he must have crossed in some miraculous manner. Wesley explains why any were still there: they were held by the want of vessels, and stayed the less unwillingly for seeing that Jesus had not embarked. Henry gives the motive plainly: their hearts being set on making him a king, they lay in wait for his return.

Where these people were standing is disputed. Barnes explains the phrase about the other side from the standpoint of a writer living on the west, and Ellicott points out that the starting point shifts within a few verses. Clarke denies they were in Perea at all, citing Bishop Pearce that the Greek word can mean on the side of as well as beyond. Calvin adds the geography behind the confusion, Tiberias lying where the lake is broadest, Bethsaida next, and Capernaum near the lowest part where the Jordan issues, so that it is directly opposite nothing. Ellicott and Robertson put the meeting in the synagogue at Capernaum, perhaps the one built by the centurion.

The question they ask is never answered, and every witness notices it. Ellicott says there is an earlier sign than the one they ask about, whose spiritual meaning neither they nor the disciples have grasped, so he passes from their curiosity to the hidden truth. Calvin says he chides them instead for pressing forward without considering why they had come, and Wesley that he begins here to try their sincerity, having until now been gathering hearers. Chrysostom defends the sharpness: the mild and gentle is not always useful, and a dull hearer must be roused with a goad, which the Son of God does here as elsewhere. Robertson notes that they had indeed seen signs, but that this one led to wild fanaticism and a complete failure to grasp what it taught.

What they are charged with is a motive rather than an error. Barnes allows that to seek Christ because the miracles proved him sent from God would have been proper, and calls following him merely because their wants were supplied a gross selfishness, adding that many still seek religion from no better motive. Clarke makes the same complaint historically: though the miracle was among the most astonishing ever wrought, and attested by all their senses, many regarded the hand of God in it no further than it satisfied their appetite. Gill notes that Christ could have told them how he came and would not gratify the curiosity.

The command that follows turns on a verb. Ellicott says the margin is much better than the text here, since work not rather than labour not preserves the connection with the questions that follow. Robertson takes the present imperative as a prohibition of the habit, and reads the perishing meat against a crowd already hungry again. Barnes and Clarke guard the saying from misuse: it forbids not effort for the supply of our wants but anxiety, and the making of this the supreme object, since our Lord would have every man diligent in the employment providence placed him in, that employment subservient to the soul's interest. Wesley states the positive side, that we work for everlasting life as well as from it, on a principle of faith and love. Calvin explains the shape of the sentence: because our understandings are gross and devoted to earthly things, the disease is corrected first and the duty pointed out after. Lightfoot closes with the rabbis on the seal of God, which one of them names Truth.
28:
The question about works is taken as a half-understanding. Ellicott says the verse confirms the sense given to the command before it, since they grasp that there are works appointed of God; Calvin agrees they understood they were called higher than the conveniences of the present life, and puts the mistake elsewhere. Robertson makes the question a deliberative subjunctive, what are we to do as a habit. Gill locates the error exactly, that they imagined eternal life was to be obtained by working. Henry notices the manner rather than the matter: Christ gave them leave to ask and did not resent the interruption as an affront.

The answer turns a plural into a singular. Ellicott puts it most sharply: they speak of works, regarding life as an aggregate of separate deeds, while he speaks of work, regarding the separate acts as the outcome of a principle, his own works making one complete work. Robertson observes that Jesus calls belief in himself the work of God, where these hearers thought of deeds of the Pharisaic sort, and compares Paul's phrase about a work of faith. Barnes is careful that this is not quietism: Jesus did not tell them they had nothing to do, but that a work remained and was imperative. Calvin adds that all men undertake without faith is vain.

The demand for a sign astonishes almost every witness. Ellicott asks whether men who had seen thousands fed the day before, and would have made him king for it, can be demanding a sign now. Robertson puts it as though the sign of the previous day were of no value. Clarke says they had seen it already and did not believe, so no miracle would have satisfied them, and Calvin quotes the saying about an evil generation that seeks after a sign.

What they want instead is manna, and two of them explain why. Robertson reports that the rabbis proved from a psalm that the Messiah when he came would outdo Moses with bread from heaven, and Lightfoot that the nation looked for the dainties their Messiah was to bring, manna above all. Ellicott states the logic: the Messiah was to be greater than Moses while the sign shown was less, what they ate being the common bread of earth however multiplied. Clarke puts their argument in their own mouths, that five thousand fed once is little beside a million fed for forty years. Wesley distinguishes two heavens, the lower sublunary one from which the manna fell and the highest, from which, as he counts, Jesus says seven times in this discourse that he came down.

The reply denies the premise twice over. Robertson calls it a blunt and pointed denial that Moses was the giver at all, and notes that the claim is to my Father rather than our Father. Clarke sets the refutation out in four steps: it was God and not Moses who gave the manna, it was not the true bread but a type, a far more excellent bread has now been given, and Christ himself is that nourishment. Calvin explains how the saying stands beside the psalm: it speaks by comparison, the manna nourishing the body where the true bread gives life to the soul.

The request that follows divides the readers. Ellicott hears the same mistake as the Samaritan woman's, a thought of physical need, and would render the address Sir rather than Lord. Calvin goes further and takes it for irony, an accusation of vain boasting, adding that men who reject the promises of God then put Christ in the place of their own unbelief. Wesley reads it the other way, that they still mean it literally yet seem now not far from believing, while Clarke leaves both doors open, a request either that the manna be renewed or that the bread just spoken of become their constant nourishment.
35:
The great sentence is felt as a shock. Robertson calls it startling in the extreme to the crowd and guards it from a false parallel: Philo compares the manna to the divine Word, but allegorically and vaguely, and this language is far removed from that. Chrysostom marks where the discourse turns, since Christ now begins to set forth mysteries and speaks first of his divinity, not of his body, which comes only at the end. Ellicott hears the answer to their request, since they had asked for this bread and it now stands present before them. Calvin makes the same point with an edge, that what they demanded in mockery is set before their eyes, and that the doctrine has two parts, whence life is to be sought and how enjoyed. Clarke and Wesley gloss the metaphor plainly, bread that gives life and preserves from death, treating coming and believing as equivalent terms.

The saying about those the Father gives divides the witnesses sharply. Robertson notes the collective neuter singular, a classical idiom carrying perhaps a notion of unity; Barnes and Clarke take the neuter for the masculine, Clarke adding the qualification that governs his whole reading, that those drawn are led and not driven, since as many as are led by the Spirit of God are the children of God. Calvin goes the other way and takes the obstinacy of these hearers as proof that they are reprobate and no part of the flock, the distinction serving to keep the authority of the doctrine unimpaired when many reject it. Wesley describes the given as those who feel themselves lost and follow the drawings of the Father, and promises them pardon, holiness and heaven if they endure to the end. Gill limits the term from both sides: it means neither the apostles only nor every individual of mankind.

The two verses on the sender's will are read as a guarantee. Robertson marks the perfect tense of the coming down; Ellicott observes that Christ identifies his own will with the Father's while still asserting that he has one of his own. Barnes takes the point to be faithfulness to a trust, so that though these hearers reject him the will of God is accomplished in the salvation of others.

On losing nothing the difference of school reappears. Calvin infers that all who do not profit by the Gospel are reprobate and willingly draw ruin on themselves, so we need not despond when many perish. Clarke draws the opposite line: God may will a thing to be without willing that it shall be, and wills perseverance without forcing it, Judas having been given to Christ and lost. Wesley takes the same view in a sentence, that the promise holds if they endure to the end, and Judas did not. Lightfoot supplies the background of the phrase about the last day, the nation looking for the resurrection at the Messiah's coming, one rabbi asking to be buried in his shirt and shoes so as to be ready.

The closing verse is treated as a deliberate safeguard. Barnes says Christ never left a doctrine so stated without guarding it, and that seeing was not enough, many Jews having seen him and few believed. Clarke makes it explicit: lest they take a wrong meaning from what went before, he tells them plainly that so far from any being excluded it is God's will that every one who sees may believe and be saved. Ellicott prefers the best manuscripts here and in the verse before, which keep the relation of Father and Son in view. Robertson makes the subjunctive continuous, that he may keep on having eternal life, and takes the beholding for the eye of faith; Calvin reduces it to a rule, that the way to salvation is to obey the Gospel; Wesley calls the verse the sum of the three before it.
41:
The murmuring is diagnosed rather than described. Robertson notes the verb is onomatopoetic, used in the Greek Old Testament of murmuring against Moses, and likens it to the cooing of doves or the buzzing of bees. Ellicott would render it murmured concerning him, and finds the true spirit of objectors in it, disregarding what has since been said and fastening on whatever they do not understand in its most startling form. Chrysostom traces the timing: while they hoped for food they could eat they had no misgivings, and the complaint began when that hope was taken away, so the reason they gave was a pretence. Calvin locates the offence in the meanness of Christ's human condition, in which they perceived nothing divine; Clarke, in the drift of the discourse, which went to prove him greater than Moses.

The saying about drawing is where the schools part. Robertson observes that the verb can mean to drag, as of a net or a sword or a man haled to court, but that here it is a drawing by moral power. Clarke seizes on that and answers with the poet's line quoted by Augustine, that every man is drawn by his own delight: show green herbage to a sheep and he is drawn, show nuts to a child and he is drawn. Wesley states the same as a balance: no man can believe unless God give him power, and God draws first by good desires, not by compulsion nor by laying the will under necessity. Calvin takes the verse the other way, as reminding them that to embrace this doctrine is a peculiar gift, said so their unbelief should not disturb weaker minds. Gill puts it flatly, that men in an unregenerate state have neither the power nor the will.

The quotation that follows is handled as a formula. Barnes, Clarke and Ellicott take the plural for the book of the prophets and refer it to Isaiah, noting that the thought runs through Jeremiah too; Calvin explains the plural by the collection of all the prophecies into one volume, so that they may be counted a single book.

The next verse is read as a guard against misunderstanding. Barnes says it was added because a pupil commonly sees his teacher, where this teaching is of another kind; Clarke, that God teaches by his Spirit and not in person. Ellicott makes the relation exact, that hearing the Father was preparation for the fuller revelation in the Son and not a substitute for it; Robertson, that since no one has seen God with the eyes, the only way to see him is to see Christ. Calvin insists both halves be joined: no knowledge of Christ can be had until the Father enlightens the naturally blind, and yet it is vain to seek God apart from Christ.

The claim is repeated with an addition. Ellicott observes that the words which seemed so hard to fathom are only the same truth cast in the form of their own demand, and marks the change from bread that is of life to bread that is living, containing the principle of life in itself. Calvin explains the repetition itself, that nothing is more necessary to be known and every man feels how hard it is to believe and how quickly it slips away. Augustine states the double reference: Christ calls himself bread not only in respect of the divinity which feeds all things but of the human nature assumed by the Word. Lightfoot hears in the last clause a quiet refutation of their expected Messianic dainties, since all the dainties Christ provided were himself. Barnes refers the giving of the flesh to the sacrifice, in the language of the institution of the Supper; Wesley enters the caution that marks his school, that the whole discourse refers directly to the passion and only remotely, if at all, to the Supper.
52:
The strife is treated as a step down from the murmuring. Robertson notes the verb is used of armed combat before a war of words, and calls the imperfect inchoative: they had been murmuring, and now began bitter contention, some probably catching a spiritual sense while others would not. Ellicott marks the advance: they now understand him to mean his flesh is to be eaten, though his words have not yet said so. Augustine turns the fact into a contrast: the Jews strove because they did not understand what the bread of peace was, where those who eat that bread do not strive, God making them dwell together in unity. Calvin says the name Jews is used not by way of honour but to reproach an unbelief that will not even inquire modestly into what it finds obscure. Wesley notes the ascending order of the chapter: the Jews tried here, the disciples next, the apostles last.

The answer raises the difficulty rather than lowering it. Barnes denies flatly that it can be literal, the thing never having been done and nothing being more absurd than to suppose it intended. Clarke gives the sense as being made partakers of the blessings purchased by the passion, keeping the analogy running: as a man must eat bread to be nourished by it, so he must receive the grace and Spirit of Christ. Wesley puts it in a line, that eating his flesh is another expression for believing. Calvin hears in the oath a just resentment at grace rejected with disdain, threatening mingled with doctrine to strike terror; Gill and Clarke note that the difficulty is not removed until the discourse ends.

On the next verse two of them correct the translation. Clarke and Robertson prefer the adjective to the adverb on the best manuscripts, so the sense is not meat indeed but true food and true drink; Ellicott renders it the same way, taking the verse as the answer to their question how this man can give them his flesh. Bede sets out what the change is for, to show the difference between bodily meat and drink and the spiritual mystery of the body and blood. Calvin supplies the comparison that makes it intelligible: as the body is consumed for want of food, so the soul perishes with hunger if not fed with heavenly bread; Wesley, that a believer's soul is as truly fed by this as the body by meat and drink.

The promise of mutual indwelling draws close attention. Clarke finds a deliberate figure, since of all unions none is so intimate as that effected by digesting food, changed into the very substance of the one who eats, and our Lord makes that the model. Ellicott prefers abideth to dwelleth and calls it one of those deeper thoughts which meet us only in the beloved disciple; Robertson, that the verb expresses a continual mystical fellowship. Calvin adds that there is no other way for Christ to become ours than by faith directed to his flesh. Henry glosses flesh and blood together as the Redeemer in the nature of man, Christ crucified and the redemption wrought by him.

The close returns to where the discourse began. Calvin says the sermon had to end this way, the comparison renewed, since there is no reason to prefer Moses to one who supplies far better food; Robertson calls the verse a final explanation of the true manna, and Ellicott notes the tense has moved into the past. Gill observes that all this was said openly in the place of public worship, and Clarke that the interruptions only gave fuller opportunity to proclaim the whole truth about the passion. Robertson reports a carved stone among the ruins of that synagogue bearing a pot of manna. Calvin ends on the count, that out of so great a multitude scarcely a few profited by it.
60:
The complaint is weighed word for word. Robertson glosses the adjective as rough, harsh, dried hard, and takes the hard saying to be the last one, that they were to eat him; Clarke renders the objection as a question about digesting such doctrine, which they found intolerable, and recalls a similar phrase in Euripides. Barnes is careful about who is speaking, since disciple means learner and does not of itself imply a real Christian; Ellicott agrees the word is used in the wider sense, though he thinks the apostles not excluded from it. Calvin puts the hardness where he thinks it belongs, in their hearts and not in the word, since the reprobate make stones of God's word to dash themselves upon, then complain of what ought to have softened them. Augustine describes the misunderstanding exactly: taking the words in a human sense, they supposed he spoke of cutting up the flesh of the Word for distribution. Wesley turns the saying around, hard to the children of the world and sweet to the children of God, and observes that scarcely ever did our Lord speak more sublimely, even to the apostles. Henry sums the effect: the discourse was to some a savour of death unto death, not to the Jews only but to disciples.

The question about the ascension is read two ways. Clarke takes it as removing the offence, since they would soon have full proof that the saying was figurative when they saw him ascend in the body he rose with. Wesley and Barnes read it the other way, Wesley asking how much more incredible the giving of his flesh would then appear, Barnes noting that instead of explaining away the offence Jesus states a further doctrine quite as offensive. Calvin finds in it a lifting of the veil, since the mean condition before their eyes had kept them from submitting to a divine power, and they are now called to behold a heavenly glory. Gill and Clarke take the preceding verse for proof of divinity, since he knew their murmuring in himself without being told; Ellicott notes the tenses put the scene in the present, his knowing and their murmuring together.

The saying about spirit and flesh is the crux, and they agree more than might be expected. Barnes denies that the word spirit here means the Holy Ghost, since the next clause makes the words themselves spirit, and refers it to the doctrine just taught; Clarke says it is the spiritual sense only that is to be attended to; Wesley makes the flesh the bare, carnal, literal meaning, which profits nothing. Robertson marks the articular participle and the contrast between spirit and flesh running through the Gospel. Calvin says this explains why the hearers did not profit, a spiritual doctrine finding no ears well prepared, and warns that the passage has been expounded in various ways.

The unbelief is treated as foreseen, not caused. Clarke applies it to Judas and those who afterwards left, adding that Christ knew from the call and from eternity. Wesley draws the line carefully, that God does foresee future contingencies while his foreknowledge is not their cause. Calvin says they corrupted a quickening doctrine for want of faith and turned it to their own ruin, which answers beforehand the objection that they felt nothing quickening in it. Robertson puts it shortest, that failure to believe kills the life in the words.

The last verse returns to the earlier saying about drawing. Robertson notes it makes the same point as before with a different verb, the impulse to faith coming from God. Ellicott gives the figure: unless the fields are prepared it is vain to sow, and the defection proves the hearts unready without touching the goodness of the seed. Calvin takes it as a caution against astonishment that the Gospel is not everywhere received, faith being an uncommon gift.
66:
The defection is read as a sifting. Wesley says our Lord now began to purge his floor, the proud and careless driven away and those remaining who were fit for the Master's use; Robertson puts it the same way, that Jesus drew the line of cleavage between true and false believers. Ellicott corrects the English, since the Greek has no word for time and probably means on that account, the departure being the result of a teaching that tested them. Gill, Clarke and Barnes limit who went: none from the twelve and none, Gill adds, from the seventy, but from the wider body that had followed and professed. Barnes draws the lesson that we need not wonder at the apostasy of many who profess to follow Christ, and Henry the warning, that when we admit hard thoughts of the words and works of Jesus we enter into a temptation which, unless mercy prevent, ends in drawing back.

The question to the twelve is heard as tender rather than cold. Clarke makes the words emphatic: will you abandon me, whom I have distinguished with innumerable marks of affection and chosen out of the world to be my companions? Robertson notes the form of the Greek expects the answer no, and wonders whether Judas showed some sympathy with the departing crowds while keeping still. Calvin gives the pastoral reason for asking at all, that the faith of the apostles might well be shaken at finding themselves so small a remnant of a great multitude, and they are shown there is no reason to be carried away by the unsteadiness of others.

Peter answers for the rest, and every witness says so. Clarke and Barnes call it characteristic, the usual zeal of the man who speaks first; Ellicott suggests the look may have been directed to him, and finds the speech striking, since they had left all to follow and found all in him. Calvin says the reply has two clauses, the first giving the reason he adheres to Christ with his brethren, and adds that all were of the same mind except that in Judas there was no sincerity. Wesley reduces the first half to its point, that Christ alone speaks the words which show the way to life everlasting. Robertson reads the whole as a choice already made, so that if desertion crossed their minds when the crowd left, they dismissed it instantly.

The confession that follows is weighed for its tenses. Robertson and Ellicott both render the verbs as perfects, we have come to believe and still believe, we have come to know and still know, Ellicott adding that the faith which first burned in their hearts has passed into the calm certainty of settled knowledge. Gill dates it from the first call and traces the growth to the miracles and the doctrine. Barnes notes that Peter says we in the name of the whole company while one among them had no such feeling.

The answer turns the confession back on them. Barnes hears the emphasis in the pronoun, that it is the greater sin to betray one who chose them in love, and Clarke that the word for devil means an accuser enlisted on Satan's side. Robertson is careful with the tense, that Jesus does not say Judas was a devil when chosen but that he is one now. Ellicott finds the brightness of that hope crossed by a shadow, seen in its full darkness by the light of the truth just spoken. Wesley reads it as a gracious warning on which Judas ought to have repented, and infers that men may fall even from such an election. Calvin thinks Christ was fortifying the eleven against an offence already at hand, and observes that Judas, for all his bad conscience, is not recorded to have been moved, hypocrites being too stupid to feel their own sores.
